citation: Hemming et al., The performance of small sample correction methods for controlling type I error when analyzing parallel cluster randomized trials: a systematic review of simulation studies
reported_findings: For continuous outcomes, cluster-level analyses with between-within degrees of freedom, mixed models with Satterthwaite correction, or Fay/Graubard-corrected GEE often preserved nominal type-I error in some settings with as few as six clusters.
Other settings required substantially more clusters; no single small-sample method is uniformly valid for all designs.
limitations: Cluster-randomized clinical/implementation data, not magnetic manufacturing.
Type-I error control does not imply adequate power or process capability.

citation: Alexeev and Morton, Cluster Trials Inference With CARE
reported_findings: Cluster-size and cluster-structure heterogeneity can distort inference.
Proposes a design-anchored benchmark before assumption-rich estimators, with sensitivity and cluster influence diagnostics.
limitations: Clinical/pragmatic cluster-trial context; manufacturing application must validate its own variance and design assumptions.

citation: Baumann et al., A tutorial on conducting sample size and power calculations for detecting treatment effect heterogeneity in cluster randomized trials with linear mixed models
reported_findings: Power calculations depend on cluster count, cluster size, covariance structure and effect heterogeneity.
The tutorial consolidates calculations for several parallel, crossover and stepped-wedge cluster designs.
limitations: Methodology source only; not a magnetic-manufacturing effect-size or sample-size authority.

citation: Small sample cluster randomized trials with a small number of clusters: which analyses should be used?
reported_findings: Uncorrected large-sample methods may inflate type-I error with small cluster counts; small-sample degrees-of-freedom corrections are important.
Some scenarios with fewer than 20 clusters had low power.
limitations: Older methodology study in healthcare context, not directly transferable to manufacturing.
